claim: A vision-language-action manipulation policy becomes markedly more robust on contact-rich multi-step tasks if its demonstrations are augmented with random arm displacements followed by motions back to the start of the next subtask, so it learns to carry on from unfamiliar arm poses, and if it is given a few learned object-reset skills that a multimodal language model switches in when it judges the scene has become unrecoverable. Supported only if, on nine RoboMimic tasks at two levels of scene randomisation, its mean success is higher than the same backbone fine-tuned normally, than the best prior self-correction method, and even than that method given human-corrected instructions; if it is best on at least eight of the nine tasks; and if on a physical arm it beats the backbone on both tasks tested.

experiments: Build the training data and system. Setup: for each of nine RoboMimic tasks (Coffee, Stack, StackThree, Threading, ThreePieceAssembly at randomisation levels D0 and D1), expand 10 human demonstrations to 500 with MimicGen and insert, at the start and between subtasks, a random arm displacement (up to 45 degrees and 0.5 m) followed by an interpolated motion back to the next subtask's start; train only on the return motion plus the following task actions, never on the random displacement. Run the resulting policy for hundreds of episodes, have Gemini-2.5-Pro label each failure video (retryable or reset-required, object to reset, interacting objects, time of failure), restore the logged simulator state at that time, collect 20 human reset demonstrations per object, place the interacting objects together in new scenes and expand to 500 with the same augmentation. Fine-tune pi0.5 with one LoRA adapter for the task and one per reset skill; at run time an online language-model monitor swaps in a reset adapter when it judges the scene unrecoverable and swaps back afterwards. 50 trials per task.

Compare with VLA and self-correction baselines on all nine tasks. Setup: fine-tuned OpenVLA; diffusion policies conditioned on the task, on predicted subgoals, or on corrected motion instructions; subgoal self-reflection; Phoenix; Phoenix with human-corrected motion instructions; and the pi0.5 backbone. Result: mean success 84.0% against 72.2% for pi0.5, 57.8% for Phoenix, 78.9% for Phoenix with human corrections and 38.0% for OpenVLA; best on eight of nine tasks, with larger gains at the more randomised D1 level (Coffee D1 78% vs 56%, ThreePieceAssembly D1 58% vs 46%); on Threading D0 it scores 72%, below the subgoal and self-reflection diffusion policies (78-80%) and human-corrected Phoenix (100%) but above pi0.5 (42%) and Phoenix (68%).

Test on a physical arm without simulator state. Setup: a Piper arm with top and wrist RealSense D435i cameras, two tasks (stack three blocks; insert a U-shaped block); 10 human demonstrations per task and per reset skill, augmented to 50 using object poses estimated by Any6D instead of simulator logs, failure states reproduced only approximately; 40 trials each. Result: 75.0% vs 62.5% for pi0.5 on stacking and 55.0% vs 45.0% on insertion.

Check sensitivity to how large the injected displacements are. Setup: on Coffee D1, vary the maximum rotation and translation of the random displacement, train on each, and record task success and the share of augmented demonstrations that generate successfully. Result: every setting beats Phoenix and pi0.5; success is best at 30 degrees rotation and 0.7 m translation; larger displacements give more varied data and higher success up to a point but lower generation efficiency, and very large ones reduce success.
